paragraphs: It was quite late (days are short in November) when Alyosha rang at the prison gate. Dusk was beginning to fall. But Alyosha knew he would be let in without trouble. Things worked in our little town the way they do everywhere. At first, of course, once the preliminary inquiry was over, relatives and a few other people could see Mitya only by going through certain unavoidable formalities. Later, though the formalities were not relaxed, exceptions were made for at least some of Mitya’s visitors. So much so that sometimes the meetings with the prisoner, in the room set aside for them, were practically _tête-à-tête_.

These exceptions were few, however. Only Grushenka, Alyosha and Rakitin were treated this way. The captain of the police, Mihail Mihailovitch, was very well disposed toward Grushenka. His abuse of her at Mokroe weighed on the old man’s conscience, and once he learned the whole story he changed his opinion of her completely. And strange to say, though he was firmly convinced of Mitya’s guilt, after Mitya was once in prison the old man came to take a more and more lenient view of him. “He was a man of good heart, perhaps,” he thought, “who came to grief through drink and dissipation.” His first horror had given way to pity. As for Alyosha, the police captain was very fond of him and had known him a long time. Rakitin, who had lately taken to visiting the prisoner very often, was one of the closest acquaintances of “the police captain’s young ladies,” as he called them, and was always hanging about their house. He gave lessons in the house of the prison superintendent, too, who, though strict in carrying out his duties, was a kind-hearted old man. Alyosha, for his part, had known the superintendent intimately for a long time, and the old man liked to talk to him, usually about sacred subjects. He respected Ivan Fyodorovitch and stood in awe of his opinion, though he was something of a philosopher himself, “self-taught,” of course. But Alyosha had an irresistible attraction for him. During the last year the old man had taken up the study of the Apocryphal Gospels, and he was always talking over his impressions with his young friend. He used to come to the monastery to see him and would spend hours discussing these things with him and with the monks. So even if Alyosha arrived late at the prison, he had only to go to the superintendent and everything was made easy. Besides, everyone in the prison, down to the humblest warder, had grown used to Alyosha. The sentry, of course, did not trouble him as long as the authorities were satisfied.

When Mitya was summoned from his cell, he always came downstairs to the place set aside for interviews. As Alyosha entered the room, he came upon Rakitin, who was just taking leave of Mitya. They were both talking loudly. Mitya was laughing heartily as he saw him out, while Rakitin seemed to be grumbling. Rakitin did not like meeting Alyosha, especially lately. He hardly spoke to him and gave him only a stiff bow. Seeing Alyosha come in now, he frowned and looked away, as though he were wholly absorbed in buttoning his big, warm, fur-trimmed overcoat. Then he began looking for his umbrella.
“I must be careful not to forget my things,” he muttered, simply to say something.
“And be careful not to forget other people’s things,” said Mitya, as a joke, and laughed at once at his own wit. Rakitin flared up instantly.
“You’d better give that advice to your own family, who’ve always been a slave-driving lot, and not to Rakitin,” he cried, suddenly shaking with anger.

“What’s the matter? I was joking,” cried Mitya. “Damn it all! They’re all like that,” he said to Alyosha, nodding toward Rakitin’s quickly retreating figure. “He was sitting here, laughing and cheerful, and all at once he boils over like that. He didn’t even nod to you. Have you broken with him completely? Why are you so late? I haven’t just been waiting, I’ve been thirsting for you the whole morning. But never mind. We’ll make up for it now.”
“Why does he come here so often? Surely you’re not such great friends?” asked Alyosha. He, too, nodded at the door through which Rakitin had disappeared.

“Great friends with Rakitin? No, not as much as that. Is it likely—with a pig like that? He thinks I’m ... a blackguard. They can’t take a joke either, that’s the worst of such people. They never understand a joke, and their souls are dry, dry and flat; they remind me of the prison walls when I was first brought here. But he’s a clever fellow, very clever. Well, Alexey, it’s all over with me now.”
He sat down on the bench and made Alyosha sit down beside him.
“Yes, the trial’s tomorrow. Are you so hopeless, brother?” Alyosha said, with a feeling of dread.

“What are you talking about?” said Mitya, looking at him a little uncertainly. “Oh, you mean the trial! Damn it all! Till now we’ve been talking about things that don’t matter, about this trial, but I haven’t said a word to you about the main thing. Yes, the trial is tomorrow; but it wasn’t the trial I meant when I said it was all over with me. Why do you look at me so critically?”
“What do you mean, Mitya?”
“Ideas, ideas, that’s all! Ethics! What is ethics?”
“Ethics?” asked Alyosha, wondering.
“Yes; is it a science?”
“Yes, there is such a science ... but ... I admit I can’t explain to you what sort of science it is.”

“Rakitin knows. Rakitin knows a lot, damn him! He’s not going to be a monk. He means to go to Petersburg. There he’ll go in for criticism with an uplifting slant. Who knows, he may be useful and make his own career, too. Ough! They’re first-rate at making a career, these people! Damn ethics, I’m done for, Alexey, I am, you man of God! I love you more than anyone. It makes my heart ache to look at you. Who was Karl Bernard?”
“Karl Bernard?” Alyosha was surprised again.
“No, not Karl. Wait, I made a mistake. Claude Bernard. What was he? A chemist or what?”
“He must be a scholar,” answered Alyosha; “but I admit I can’t tell you much about him, either. I’ve heard of him as a scholar, but what sort, I don’t know.”

“Well, damn him, then! I don’t know either,” swore Mitya. “Some sort of scoundrel, most likely. They’re all scoundrels. And Rakitin will make his way. Rakitin will get on anywhere; he’s another Bernard. Ugh, these Bernards! They’re all over the place.”
“But what is the matter?” Alyosha asked insistently.

“He wants to write an article about me, about my case, and so begin his literary career. That’s what he comes for; he said so himself. He wants to prove some theory. He wants to say ‘he couldn’t help murdering his father, he was corrupted by his environment,’ and so on. He explained it all to me. He’s going to put in a touch of Socialism, he says. But there, damn the fellow, he can put in a touch if he likes, I don’t care. He can’t stand Ivan, he hates him. He’s not fond of you, either. But I don’t throw him out, because he’s a clever fellow. Awfully conceited, though. I said to him just now, ‘The Karamazovs aren’t blackguards, they’re philosophers; for all true Russians are philosophers, and though you’ve studied, you’re not a philosopher—you’re a low fellow.’ He laughed, so maliciously. And I said to him, ‘_De ideabus non est disputandum_.’ Isn’t that rather good? I can set myself up as a classicist, you see!” Mitya laughed suddenly.
“Why is it all over with you? You said so just now,” Alyosha put in.
“Why is it all over with me? H’m!... The fact is ... taking it all together, I’m sorry to lose God—that’s why.”
“What do you mean by ‘sorry to lose God’?”

“Imagine: inside, in the nerves, in the head—that is, these nerves are there in the brain ... (damn them!) there are sort of little tails, the little tails of those nerves, and as soon as they start quivering ... that is, you see, I look at something with my eyes and then they start quivering, those little tails ... and when they quiver, an image appears ... it doesn’t appear at once, but an instant, a second, goes by ... and then something like a moment appears; that is, not a moment—devil take the moment!—but an image; that is, an object, or an action, damn it! That’s why I see and then think, because of those tails, not at all because I’ve got a soul, or because I’m some sort of image and likeness. All that is nonsense! Rakitin explained it all to me yesterday, brother, and it simply knocked me over. It’s magnificent, Alyosha, this science! A new man is rising—that I understand.... And yet I’m sorry to lose God!”
“Well, that’s a good thing, anyway,” said Alyosha.

“That I’m sorry to lose God? It’s chemistry, brother, chemistry! There’s no help for it, your reverence, you’ll have to make way for chemistry. And Rakitin does dislike God. Ough! Doesn’t he dislike Him! That’s the sore spot with all of them. But they hide it. They lie. They pretend. ‘Will you preach this in your reviews?’ I asked him. ‘Oh, well, if I did it openly, they wouldn’t let it through,’ he said. He laughed. ‘But what will become of men then?’ I asked him, ‘without God and immortal life? All things are lawful then, they can do what they like?’ ‘Didn’t you know?’ he said, laughing, ‘a clever man can do what he likes,’ he said. ‘A clever man knows his way around, but you’ve put your foot in it, committing a murder, and now you’re rotting in prison.’ He says that to my face! A regular pig! I used to kick such people out, but now I listen to them. He talks a lot of sense, too. Writes well. He began reading me an article last week. I copied out three lines of it. Wait a minute. Here it is.”
Mitya hurriedly pulled a piece of paper out of his pocket and read:
“‘In order to settle this question, it is above all essential to set one’s personality in contradiction to one’s reality.’ Do you understand that?”
“No, I don’t,” said Alyosha. He looked at Mitya and listened to him with curiosity.

“I don’t understand either. It’s dark and obscure, but intellectual. ‘Everyone writes like that now,’ he says, ‘it’s the effect of their environment.’ They’re afraid of the environment. He writes poetry, too, the rascal. He’s written some in honor of Madame Hohlakov’s foot. Ha ha ha!”
“I’ve heard about it,” said Alyosha.
“Have you? And have you heard the poem?”
“No.”

“I’ve got it. Here it is. I’ll read it to you. You don’t know—I haven’t told you—there’s quite a story about it. He’s a rascal! Three weeks ago he started to tease me. ‘You’ve got yourself into a mess, like a fool, for the sake of three thousand, but I’m going to grab a hundred and fifty thousand. I’m going to marry a widow and buy a house in Petersburg.’ And he told me he was courting Madame Hohlakov. She didn’t have much brains in her youth, and now at forty she’s lost what she had. ‘But she’s awfully sentimental,’ he says; ‘that’s how I’ll get hold of her. When I marry her, I’ll take her to Petersburg and there I’ll start a newspaper.’ And his mouth was simply watering, the beast, not for the widow, but for the hundred and fifty thousand. And he made me believe it. He came to see me every day. ‘She’s coming round,’ he declared. He was beaming with delight. And then, all of a sudden, he was thrown out of the house. Perhotin’s carrying everything before him, bravo! I could kiss the silly old noodle for throwing him out. And he’d written this doggerel. ‘It’s the first time I’ve dirtied my hands writing poetry,’ he said. ‘It’s to win her heart, so it’s in a good cause. When I get hold of the silly woman’s fortune, I can be of great social use.’ They always have this social excuse for every nasty thing they do! ‘Anyway it’s better than your Pushkin’s poetry,’ he said, ‘for I’ve managed to advocate enlightenment even in that.’ I understand what he means about Pushkin, I quite see that, if Pushkin really was a man of talent and only wrote about women’s feet. But wasn’t Rakitin puffed up about his doggerel! The vanity of these fellows! ‘On the convalescence of the swollen foot of the object of my affections’—that’s what he thought of for a title. He’s a waggish fellow.
A captivating little foot, Though swollen and red and tender! The doctors come and plasters put, But still they cannot mend her.
Yet it’s not for her foot I dread— A theme for Pushkin’s muse more fit— It’s not her foot, it is her head: I tremble for her loss of wit!
For as her foot swells, strange to say, Her intellect is on the wane— Oh, for some remedy I pray That may restore both foot and brain!
He’s a pig, a regular pig, but he’s very sly, the rascal! And he really has put in a progressive idea. And wasn’t he angry when she kicked him out! He was grinding his teeth!”
“He’s taken his revenge already,” said Alyosha. “He’s written a paragraph about Madame Hohlakov.”
And Alyosha told him briefly about the paragraph in _Gossip_.

“That’s his doing, that’s his doing!” Mitya agreed, frowning. “That’s him! These paragraphs ... I know ... the insulting things that have been written about Grushenka, for instance.... And about Katya, too.... H’m!”
He walked across the room with a harassed air.

“Brother, I can’t stay long,” Alyosha said, after a pause. “Tomorrow will be a great and awful day for you, the judgment of God will be carried out ... I’m amazed at you, you walk about here, talking of I don’t know what ...”

“No, don’t be amazed at me,” Mitya broke in warmly. “Am I to talk about that stinking dog? About the murderer? We’ve talked enough about him. I don’t want to say any more about the stinking son of Stinking Lizaveta! God will kill him, you’ll see. Hush!”
He went up to Alyosha excitedly and kissed him. His eyes glowed.

“Rakitin wouldn’t understand this,” he began in a sort of exaltation; “but you, you’ll understand it all. That’s why I was thirsting for you. You see, there’s so much I’ve wanted to tell you for ever so long, here, within these peeling walls, but I haven’t said a word about what matters most; the moment never seemed to come. Now I can’t wait any longer. I must pour out my heart to you. Brother, these last two months I’ve found a new man in myself. A new man has risen up in me. He was hidden in me, but he would never have come to the surface if it hadn’t been for this blow from heaven. I’m afraid! And what do I care if I spend twenty years in the mines, breaking ore with a hammer? I’m not a bit afraid of that—it’s something else I’m afraid of now: that the new man may leave me. Even there, in the mines, underground, I may find a human heart in another convict and murderer beside me, and I may make friends with him, for even there one can live and love and suffer. One can thaw and revive a frozen heart in that convict, one can wait on him for years, and at last bring up from the dark depths a lofty soul, a feeling, suffering creature; one can bring forth an angel, create a hero! There are so many of them, hundreds of them, and we’re all to blame for them. Why did I dream of that ‘babe’ at such a moment? ‘Why is the babe so poor?’ That was a sign to me at that moment. It’s for the babe I’m going. Because we’re all responsible for all. For all the ‘babes,’ for there are big children as well as little children. All are ‘babes.’ I go for all, because someone must go for all. I didn’t kill father, but I’ve got to go. I accept it. It’s all come to me here, here, within these peeling walls. There are numbers of them there, hundreds of them underground, with hammers in their hands. Oh, yes, we’ll be in chains and there’ll be no freedom, but then, in our great sorrow, we’ll rise again to joy, without which man cannot live nor God exist, for God gives joy: it’s His privilege—a grand one. Ah, man should be dissolved in prayer! What would I be underground there without God? Rakitin’s laughing! If they drive God from the earth, we’ll shelter Him underground. One can’t exist in prison without God; it’s even more impossible than out of prison. And then we men underground will sing from the bowels of the earth a glorious hymn to God, with Whom is joy. Hail to God and His joy! I love Him!”
